title: Vision-Language-Action Models
full_title: Vision-Language-Action Models: Robot Foundation Models for Manipulation
tagline: Teaching robot arms from demonstrations: imitation learning, teleoperation and datasets, action representations, diffusion and flow policies, VLA architectures, fine-tuning, evaluation and deployment
summary: A vision-language-action model is a neural network that takes camera images and an instruction in words and outputs robot actions. The course starts from behaviour cloning, covers how demonstration data is collected and stored, compares ways of representing actions — discrete tokens, action chunks, diffusion and flow matching — and then studies the architectures that build a robot policy on a pretrained vision-language model, how they are fine-tuned for a new arm, how they are evaluated, and how they run in real time.
overview: For most of the history of robotics a robot arm did exactly what a programmer wrote down: move to this pose, close the gripper, move to that pose. Learned policies replace the program with a function trained from examples, mapping what the robot sees to what it does. Vision-language-action (VLA) models push this to its current limit: they start from a vision-language model pretrained on the web, so that they already know what a mug or a drawer looks like and what "put it away" means, and they are trained further on robot demonstrations to output joint or end-effector commands.

The course is organised around the pipeline of such a system. It begins with imitation learning and the failure modes of naive behaviour cloning, then turns to data: teleoperation rigs, demonstration quality and the large multi-robot datasets now shared between labs. It treats the representation of actions in detail, because this choice — discretised tokens, chunks of future actions, or continuous actions generated by diffusion or flow matching — decides how smooth and how fast a policy is. The central chapters dissect VLA architectures, then cover fine-tuning a pretrained model to a new arm and task, evaluating policies honestly in simulation and on hardware, and deploying them with acceptable latency and safeguards.

The field moves quickly, and model names in this course will date; the ideas — distribution shift, multimodal action distributions, the trade-off between generality and precision, and the cost of real-world data — are more stable. Figures that change with time (model sizes, dataset sizes, success rates) are given with the year they refer to.
outcomes: Explain behaviour cloning, compounding error and distribution shift, and describe remedies such as DAgger and action chunking.
Design a teleoperation and data-collection setup and specify the observations, actions and metadata a demonstration dataset must record.
Compare discretised-token, chunked, diffusion and flow-matching action representations by smoothness, multimodality and inference cost.
Describe how a VLA model attaches an action output to a pretrained vision-language backbone, and explain the role of each component.
Fine-tune a pretrained VLA policy on demonstrations from a new arm, choosing between full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Evaluate a manipulation policy in simulation and on hardware with controlled trials, success metrics and generalisation tests.
Deploy a learned policy on a real arm within its control-rate and latency budget, with safety limits enforced below the policy.

chapters.title: Imitation learning for manipulation
chapters.summary: Behaviour cloning, compounding error and distribution shift, DAgger, and why multimodal demonstrations break mean-squared-error policies.

chapters.title: Teleoperation and demonstration data
chapters.summary: Leader–follower arms, VR and spacemouse teleoperation, demonstration quality, dataset formats and large multi-robot datasets.

chapters.title: Representing actions
chapters.summary: Joint versus end-effector actions, discretised action tokens, action chunking, and the control rate a representation supports.

chapters.title: Diffusion and flow-matching policies
chapters.summary: Generating continuous action chunks by denoising diffusion and flow matching, and why they capture multimodal behaviour.

chapters.title: VLA architectures
chapters.summary: Vision-language backbones, action tokens and action experts; RT-2, OpenVLA, π0 and their successors compared.

chapters.title: Training and fine-tuning VLAs
chapters.summary: Pretraining mixtures, co-training with web data, cross-embodiment training, and full and low-rank fine-tuning for a new arm.

chapters.title: Evaluating robot policies
chapters.summary: Success metrics, controlled real-world trials, simulation benchmarks, generalisation tests and the sim-to-real gap.

chapters.title: Deploying a VLA on a real arm
chapters.summary: Inference latency and asynchronous execution, quantisation, action smoothing, and safety limits enforced below the learned policy.

history.title: ALVINN
history.detail: Dean Pomerleau's ALVINN, a small neural network trained on recordings of a human driver, steers a test vehicle at Carnegie Mellon — an early demonstration of behaviour cloning.

history.title: DAgger
history.detail: Stéphane Ross, Geoffrey Gordon and Andrew Bagnell show that querying an expert on the states a learned policy actually visits removes the compounding error of behaviour cloning.

history.title: RT-1
history.detail: Google's Robotics Transformer is trained on about 130,000 real demonstrations collected over 17 months with a fleet of mobile manipulators.

history.title: Diffusion Policy and ACT
history.detail: Diffusion Policy (Chi et al.) generates robot action sequences by denoising, and ACT with the low-cost ALOHA rig (Zhao et al.) introduces action chunking for fine bimanual tasks.

history.title: RT-2 and Open X-Embodiment
history.detail: RT-2 fine-tunes a web-scale vision-language model to output actions as tokens, coining the term vision-language-action model; the Open X-Embodiment collaboration pools data from 22 robot types.

history.title: OpenVLA and π0
history.detail: OpenVLA releases an open 7-billion-parameter VLA, and Physical Intelligence's π0 pairs a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert for dexterous tasks.
